01: TIROS-1, the first weather satellite, is launched from Cape Canaveral. In two and a half months it sends back 23,000 pictures of the Earth, 19,000 of them usable for weather analysis.
Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne found the Apple Computer Company as a partnership in Los Altos, California.
02: Walter Chrysler is born in Wamego, Kansas. He spent years as a roundhouse mechanic on Western railroads before turning to cars, and founded the Chrysler Corporation in 1925.
03: The first Pony Express rider leaves St. Joseph, Missouri, for Sacramento, about 1,900 miles away. Mail crossed in some 10 days; the telegraph ended the service after 18 months.
On a Manhattan sidewalk, Motorola's Martin Cooper makes the first call from a handheld cell phone, a 2.5-pound prototype. He calls his rival at AT&T.
04: Bill Gates and Paul Allen found Microsoft in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to sell their BASIC for the Altair 8800.
05: An F5 tornado strikes Tupelo, Mississippi, killing more than 200 people. Among the survivors is one-year-old Elvis Presley.
06: Early Bird (Intelsat I) is launched: the first commercial communications satellite in geosynchronous orbit, carrying television and telephone calls across the Atlantic.
07: U.S. carrier planes sink the Japanese battleship Yamato, the heaviest ever built, south of Kyushu with at least 11 torpedoes and 6 bombs. About 3,055 of her 3,332 men are lost.
IBM announces the System/360: a whole family of computers, small to large, that all run the same programs.
08: Mary Hawes of Burroughs gathers computer makers, users and academics, Grace Hopper among them, at the University of Pennsylvania to plan a common business language. It became COBOL.
09: Maj. Gen. Edward King surrenders the U.S. and Filipino force on Bataan. Some 75,000 prisoners are driven north on the 65-mile Bataan Death March.
10: Nebraska keeps the first Arbor Day, the idea of J. Sterling Morton of Nebraska City. An estimated one million trees are planted across the state.
Shortly after noon the new liner Titanic leaves Southampton, England, on her maiden voyage to New York.
11: Apollo 13 lifts off for the Moon. Two days out an oxygen tank explodes: 'Houston, we've had a problem.' Lovell, Swigert and Haise got home safely on April 17.
12: President Roosevelt dies and Harry Truman of Independence, Missouri, vice president for 82 days, is sworn in. He said it felt 'like the moon, the stars, and all the planets had fallen on me.'
Yuri Gagarin orbits the Earth once in Vostok 1, a flight of 108 minutes: the first human in space. Twenty years later to the day, Space Shuttle Columbia made the first shuttle flight.
13: George Westinghouse is granted U.S. patent 88,929 for the railway air brake. Today's train brakes still descend from his design.
14: Black Sunday: one of the worst dust storms in American history rolls over the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles. A reporter's story on it gave the region its name: the Dust Bowl.
At a broadcasters' convention in Chicago, Ampex demonstrates its videotape recorder, replaying a speech moments after it ended. It took $2 million in orders in four days.
15: The Titanic sinks at 2:20 a.m., two hours and forty minutes after striking an iceberg. Of more than 2,200 aboard, about 1,500 die; the Carpathia rescues 710.
16: Wilbur Wright is born near Millville, Indiana, four years before his brother Orville.
17: Ford introduces the Mustang at the New York World's Fair, priced from $2,368. Dealers take 22,000 orders the first day.
18: Lt. Col. Jimmy Doolittle leads 16 B-25 bombers off the carrier USS Hornet to bomb Tokyo and other cities. None of the planes could return to the ship; most crews came down in China.
19: Electronics magazine publishes Gordon Moore's article observing that the number of components on a chip doubles about every year: Moore's Law.
20: Apollo 16's lunar module Orion lands on the Moon with John Young and Charles Duke.
21: Manfred von Richthofen, the 'Red Baron', is shot down and killed over France. He was credited with 80 victories; historians think ground fire, not another pilot, brought him down.
22: The first railroad bridge across the Mississippi opens at Rock Island, Illinois. Two weeks later a steamboat hit it, and the railroads hired Abraham Lincoln to defend the bridge in court.
At noon about 50,000 settlers race into Oklahoma to claim two million acres. By sundown Guthrie and Oklahoma City each hold some 10,000 people.
23: Brunel's Great Western, the first steamship built for the Atlantic, reaches New York after 15 days. The smaller Sirius, which left four days earlier, beat her in by one day.
24: Space Shuttle Discovery carries the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. Its mirror proved to be ground to the wrong shape; astronauts fitted corrective optics in December 1993.
25: Elbe Day: American and Soviet soldiers meet at the Elbe River near Torgau, cutting Germany in two.
26: The converted tanker Ideal X leaves Port Newark, New Jersey, for Houston carrying 58 containers, with 58 trucks waiting at the other end: the first successful container ship.
The Baltimore and Ohio's Royal Blue makes its last run between Washington and Jersey City. In 1895 a Royal Blue train was the first in America hauled by an electric locomotive.
27: Samuel Morse is born in Charlestown, Massachusetts. He made his name as a portrait painter before the telegraph.
The steamboat Sultana, of the St. Louis to New Orleans run, explodes on the Mississippi above Memphis with 2,127 aboard, most of them freed Union prisoners. Some 1,164 die.
28: Fletcher Christian leads the mutiny on HMS Bounty. Captain Bligh and 18 loyal men are set adrift in an open boat, which Bligh sails more than 3,500 nautical miles to Timor.
29: Eli Janney of Alexandria, Virginia, is granted U.S. patent 138,405 for his knuckle coupler, which let cars couple without a man standing between them.
The last Oldsmobile, an Alero signed by the assembly-line workers, leaves the plant in Lansing, Michigan, ending a name that began in 1897.
30: Casey Jones dies at Vaughan, Mississippi, braking his Illinois Central passenger train to the last before it hits a stalled freight. He is the only one killed.
The Louisiana Purchase Exposition, the St. Louis World's Fair, opens in Forest Park. President Theodore Roosevelt starts it by telegraph from the White House.
